title: Borrowing
intro: A reference `&value` lets a function look at a value without taking ownership. The caller keeps the value, nothing is copied, and the compiler checks that the reference never outlives what it points at.

coming_from.go: `&nums` is the Rust way to pass a slice: the function sees the same elements and nothing is copied. A Go `[]int` is closest to `&mut [i32]`, since the function can write to the elements. Rust's `&[i32]` is the read-only form, and the compiler also checks that the reference never outlives `nums`.
coming_from.kotlin: A `&[i32]` parameter is like Kotlin's read-only `List<Int>`: the function can read but not add or remove. In Kotlin that is only a read-only view, so whoever holds the `MutableList` can still change it. In Rust no other code can change it while the borrow lasts (for ordinary types).
coming_from.python: Python passes a reference to every argument, so a function can change the caller's list. In Rust you choose: `&nums` lends the list for reading, `&mut nums` lends it for changing, and plain `nums` gives it away for good. A function taking `&[i32]` can only read it.
coming_from.typescript: A `&[i32]` parameter is like `readonly number[]`, but stricter. `readonly` is only a compile-time check on that one name, and another name for the same array can still change it. In Rust no other code can change it while the borrow lasts (for ordinary types).
coming_from.java: Java hands every object to a method as a reference, so `total(nums)` looks the same. In Rust you write the `&` yourself, and a `&` reference can't change the list at all. Java has no read-only reference type: a `final` variable can't be reassigned, but the list it holds can still change. The compiler also checks the reference never outlives `nums`.
coming_from.csharp: A `List<int>` variable already holds a reference, so the callee sees the same list. The closest typed match for `&[i32]` is `IReadOnlyList<int>` or `ReadOnlySpan<int>`: the function can read but not add. Rust goes further: no other code can change the list while the borrow lasts (for ordinary types). A function that takes `Vec<i32>` by value takes ownership, and the caller loses it.
coming_from.c: `&[i32]` is `const int *` plus a length, in one value. What C leaves to convention, Rust checks: the function can't write through it, can't free the array, and can't keep it past the array's life. No other code can change or free the array while it's borrowed (in safe Rust, for ordinary types).
coming_from.cpp: `&[i32]` is `std::span<const int>`, and `&T` is `const T&`. Passing a `std::vector` by value copies it; a Rust `Vec<i32>` by value moves, so the caller's `nums` is gone, and a copy only happens if you write `.clone()`. Unlike a `const T&` or a `span`, a reference in safe Rust can't dangle: the compiler rejects code where it could outlive the value.

notes: A reference is an address. `&nums` for a `Vec` is 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine; handed to a function that takes `&[i32]` it becomes 16: an address and a length. The elements stay where they are on the heap (see [the stack and the heap](/learn/stack-heap/)), and the function never gets a copy.
A `&` reference lets you read, not change (for ordinary types). Any number of them can exist at once. Changing a value through a reference needs `&mut`, in the [next lesson](/learn/mutable-borrows/).
A borrow lasts until its last use, and the value must still exist then. The compiler rejects a reference that could outlive what it points to.
`&[i32]` (a slice: an address and a length) is the usual parameter type for a list. It accepts `&Vec<i32>`, an array, or part of either. In the same way, `&str` accepts `&String`.
The signature tells you what happens to your value: `fn f(x: T)` takes it, `fn f(x: &T)` borrows it to read, `fn f(x: &mut T)` borrows it to change.

gotcha.title: A function that takes the value instead of borrowing it
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, passing a slice to a function copies the small slice header. The caller still has its slice afterwards.
gotcha.rust_sees: `xs: Vec<i32>` means "give me the Vec". Calling `total(nums)` moves the list into the function. When `total` ends, it owns the list, so the list is freed there.
gotcha.why: Nothing is wrong with the idea of reading a list twice. Rust just makes the signature say what happens to the value: `Vec<i32>` means "give me the list", and the other languages hand over a reference or a copy without asking. By the time `println!` runs, the list was freed when `total` returned. The fix is not `.clone()`. It is to say what you meant: the function only needs to look, so it borrows. (The compiler's `note:` says the same thing. Its `help:` suggests the simplest fix, not always the best one: `.clone()` would compile, but it copies the list for no reason.)

go.says: Go runs this and prints 6 [1 2 3]. Passing a slice shares the same array, so the caller can keep using it. The function could also have written to it, and nothing in the signature says whether it will.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints 6 [1, 2, 3]. The function gets a reference to the same list, so the caller can keep using it.

python.says: Python prints 6 [1, 2, 3]. Passing a list hands the function a reference to the same list, so the caller can keep using it. Nothing in the signature says whether `total` may change the list.
python.code:
def total(xs: list[int]) -> int:
    result = 0
    for x in xs:
        result += x
    return result


nums = [1, 2, 3]
t = total(nums)
print(t, nums)

typescript.says: Prints 6 [ 1, 2, 3 ]. `total` gets a reference to the same array, and the caller keeps using it. Without `readonly` in the signature, nothing says whether `total` may change the array.

java.says: Java passes a reference to the same list, and the garbage collector keeps it alive. So `nums` is still usable after the call.

csharp.says: Passing a List passes a reference, so nums is still usable after the call. The catch is that Total could also change it, and nothing in the signature says it won't.

c.says: C passes the array as a pointer, so `nums` stays usable. Nothing in the type says whether `total` may keep or free it.

cpp.says: Taking `std::vector<int>` by value makes a full copy, so `nums` is still usable and this prints `6 [1, 2, 3]`. It works, but you pay for the copy.
